summary: Describes achieving Service Function Chaining in an MPLS network by mapping the fields of the Network Service Header to an MPLS label stack. It does not replace NSH, but supports interim deployment in existing MPLS networks. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Packets need to visit several helpers in order. This uses existing labels on the packet as the instructions, so old networks can do it.

questions: what is mpls service function chaining
how does sfc work without nsh
what are sfc context label and sf label
subtitle: Carrying Service Function Chaining information in ordinary MPLS labels instead of the Network Service Header.

tldr.problem: Service Function Chaining normally uses the Network Service Header (NSH), but many existing MPLS networks do not support it and need an interim way to steer packets through ordered service functions.
tldr.mechanism: The NSH fields are mapped onto MPLS label stack entries: a two-label basic unit (an SFC Context Label and an SF Label) is used either with label swapping or with label stacking, and extended special-purpose labels carry metadata.
tldr.outcome: It does not replace the NSH. It is a compromise that lacks the NSH O bit and per-packet metadata, and it adds no new security mechanisms.

facts.label: SI position
facts.value: Top 8 bits of the Label field, low 12 bits zero

today: RFC 8595 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, and it explicitly does not replace the NSH defined in RFC 8300.

sections.title: Chaining Services with MPLS Labels
sections.content:
Service Function Chaining (SFC) directs packets through an ordered set of Service Functions (SFs) before they reach their destination. The architecture is in RFC 7665. The ordered set of SFs is a Service Function Path (SFP), and packets move between Service Function Forwarders (SFFs) that hand them to SFs and on to the next SFF. A classifier attaches the information that says which path a packet is on and how far along it is.

The Network Service Header (NSH) in RFC 8300 normally carries that information. It holds a Service Path Identifier (SPI), a Service Index (SI) and a Time To Live (TTL). RFC 8595 instead describes a logical representation of the NSH in an MPLS label stack. The NSH is not used, and its fields are mapped to MPLS labels.

This does not deprecate or replace the NSH. It acknowledges a possible need for interim SFC deployment in brownfield networks. It leaves out the O bit of RFC 8300 and has limits on metadata. The RFC describes five use cases: plain label swapping, hierarchical encapsulation by stacking, fine control over which SF instance is used, micro chains of one SF each, and Segment Routing (SR-MPLS), which is functionally the same as the micro-chain case.

Both ends of a tunnel between adjacent SFFs must know the tunnel carries SFC and which NSH representation is used. The encoding is independent of the tunnel technology, so the MPLS representation can run over a non-MPLS tunnel, and MPLS tunnels can carry the real NSH.
sections.eli5: A chain of helpers each does one job on a parcel, in order. Normally a special tag on the parcel says where it is in the chain. This RFC writes the same information using the label stickers that many networks already read.

sections.title: The Basic Unit of Two Labels
sections.content:
The building block is a pair of MPLS label stack entries. The first holds the SFC Context Label, which gives context within the SFC scope. The second holds the SF Label, which shows which SF is to be actioned. The pair can appear once or several times in a stack.

  • Label: a 20-bit integer. Its meaning depends on whether swapping or stacking is used.
  • TC: has no meaning. It SHOULD be zero when sending and MUST be ignored on receipt.
  • S: clear in the SFC Context Label entry. In the SF Label entry it is clear except at the bottom of the stack, where it MUST be set.
  • TTL: in the SFC Context Label entry it SHOULD be 1. The SF Label TTL (the SF TTL) depends on the mode and helps mitigate packet loops.
sections.eli5: Each instruction is written on two stickers. One sticker says which chain, and the other says which helper. Both have the usual sticker boxes, but one of them (the traffic class box) is simply ignored.

sections.title: Label Swapping Mode
sections.content:
In swapping mode the tunnel labels come first, then an optional entropy label, then one basic unit that acts like the NSH. The context entry is the SPI Label and the SF entry is the SI Label. The SPI keeps its RFC 8300 meaning, but a label has only 20 bits and values 0 through 15 are special-purpose, so SPI values MUST NOT be greater than 2^20 - 1 or less than 16. The SI needs 8 bits and is carried in the top 8 bits of the Label field with the low-order 12 bits set to zero.

The classifier sets the SPI Label to identify the path and the SI Label to the first SF. At each step an SFF uses the SPI Label to find the path and the SI Label to choose where to send the packet. The SPI value normally stays the same, while the SI Label is changed to point at the next hop.

The SF TTL mirrors the NSH TTL. The classifier MUST set it between 1 and 255, SHOULD base it on the expected number of SFs, and notes that the practical limit may be 63. An SFF MUST discard packets arriving with TTL zero, MUST decrement the TTL by one each time it does a lookup to forward to the next SFF, and MUST discard the packet if it reaches zero. It SHOULD log these discards but MUST rate limit the logs. SFIs ignore the TTL but mirror it back unmodified. No component may increase the SF TTL, otherwise loops may go undetected.
sections.eli5: The parcel carries one chain number and a counter. Each helper station changes the counter so the next station knows what comes next. A separate countdown stops the parcel from going around forever.

sections.title: Label Stacking and Mixed Mode
sections.content:
In stacking mode the classifier pushes one or more basic units, and together they spell out the whole path. The SFC Context Label carries the SPI (again from 16 up to 2^20 - 1) and may carry other context, such as how to read the SF Label. The SF Label identifies the next SF instance, scoped globally or within the preceding context label, from the range 16 to 2^20 - 1. TTLs SHOULD be 1 but MAY be larger if the label means forwarding toward the node that hosts the SF.

An SFF looks at the top basic unit to decide where to send the packet. If the next recipient is a local SFI, the SFF strips that unit before forwarding.

Mixed mode: a network can use both swapping and stacking, for example when a classifier wants to pin one choice of SF instance inside an installed path. The SFF checks the incoming interface and the top label to see which kind of label pair it holds. When the packet comes back from the SF, it either sets a new {SPI, SI} pair, pops the pair and tunnels to the SFF named by the context label, or pops a stacked pair and acts on whatever pair is revealed.

For SF instances that cannot process the encapsulation, an SFC proxy removes and re-imposes it. This works the same way as with the NSH.
sections.eli5: Instead of one tag that changes along the way, the parcel can carry the entire list of stops at the start. Each station peels off its own part of the list. A mix of both styles is allowed too.

sections.title: Metadata and Entropy
sections.content:
Metadata is context information exchanged between classifiers and SFs. This encoding supports per-SFP and per-flow metadata, but not per-packet metadata, which only the NSH supports.

Metadata is marked using the extended special-purpose label mechanism: an Extension Label (value 15), a Metadata Label Indicator (MLI, value 16) and then a Metadata Label that indexes a table of metadata. The table can be programmed out of band, or in band with a packet that has a Metadata Present Indicator (MPI, value 17) and carries the metadata after the bottom of the label stack, formatted as a TLV with a Length, a Metadata Type from the NSH MD Types registry, and the metadata padded to a 4-octet boundary.

In-band metadata is vulnerable to packet loss and attack. Mitigations include raising an alarm or discarding, and retransmission at a configurable interval. If metadata is changed it is RECOMMENDED to install a new entry with a new MPI. Applications sensitive to this SHOULD NOT use in-band distribution and should use control-plane or management-plane mechanisms.

For ECMP (equal-cost multipath) load balancing, the RFC RECOMMENDS an entropy label immediately after the tunnel labels and before the SFC labels, so that deep label stacks do not prevent a correct entropy hash.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a parcel needs a note with extra details. A special sticker says a note is attached or points to a note already filed. Notes can get lost in transit, so important ones are better sent by a safer route.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In the swapping example, the path has SPI 239. The classifier imposes SPI 239 and SI 255. SFFa sends the packet to SFa, then changes the SI to 254 and forwards it to SFFb. SFFb sends it to SFb, changes the SI to 253, sees it is the last SFF, strips the two SFC label entries and forwards the payload to the destination D.

In the stacking example, no forwarding state for the path is installed in the network. The classifier imposes two basic units, one for SFx and one for SFy. SFFx strips the top unit after SFx has done its work and routes toward SFFy using the revealed unit. SFFy strips the last unit and forwards the payload toward D.
sections.eli5: With swapping, the parcel's counter goes 255, 254, 253 as it passes each helper. With stacking, the parcel carries a list and each helper tears off its line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The normative security requirements of RFC 7665 and RFC 8300 apply. The classifier is a fully trusted element, and MPLS assumes packets follow the path set by the node that imposes the labels. MPLS has no built-in security and no cryptographic integrity protection on its headers, so the design relies on three principles: the MPLS network is usually a closed network, the underlying transport (for example Ethernet) may offer its own protection, and SFC-capable devices are responsible for protecting payloads. Packets originating outside or leaving the SFC domain MUST be dropped if they contain an NSH, and the same constraint applies to this MPLS encoding.

Where a tunnel links two non-MPLS domains, the tunnel design must say how it is secured. Control and management planes must also be secured, because their vulnerabilities become vulnerabilities of the whole SFC system. The RFC states that no known new vulnerabilities are introduced beyond those of the SFC architecture and the NSH specification.
sections.eli5: The system trusts the people at the front door and assumes the network is private. The labels have no lock on them, so the network's boundaries and the things underneath have to provide the security.

sections.title: IANA Label Allocations
sections.content: IANA allocated two values from the Extended Special-Purpose MPLS Label Values subregistry: 16 for the Metadata Label Indicator (MLI) and 17 for the Metadata Present Indicator (MPI). Both reference RFC 8595.
sections.eli5: Two special sticker numbers were reserved in the official list so no one else uses them for something different.

fields.name: SFC Context Label
fields.desc: Context within the SFC scope; the SPI in swapping mode.

fields.name: TC
fields.desc: No meaning; SHOULD be zero, MUST be ignored.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: MUST be clear in this entry.

fields.name: SF Label
fields.desc: Which SF is to be actioned; the SI in swapping mode.

fields.name: TC
fields.desc: No meaning; SHOULD be zero, MUST be ignored.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Clear unless this is the bottom of the stack.

fields.name: TTL
fields.desc: The SF TTL, decremented per SFF in swapping mode.
